newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore refinery profits return, but seen a blip.
newsitem.headline: Singapore refinery profits return, but seen a blip.

text.p: Singapore refining profits turned positive on Monday after crude plunged, but gains could be just a blip, industry sources said.
They said high stocks and weak demand would drive refinery margins -- the difference between crude feedstock prices and product output prices accounting for costs -- back into the red.
"Margins temporarily look brilliant because the products haven't caught up yet," a senior crude trader at a major oil company said. "But that correction will happen today."
On Friday, NYMEX crude shed 87 cents in New York to $18.79 per barrel -- its lowest price in 16 months.
Brent crude on London's International Petroleum Exchange lost 62-cents to $17.70, breaking a psychological support price of $18.00.
The fall widened the price difference with products and eased refiners profit margins.

"The drop in crude has turned margins positive...secondary margins are now about 50-60 cents in the black," a source at a Singapore refinery said, referring to the profit margin on more sophisticated refining methods.
"It is a relief because over the last two weeks we have been losing about $1 a barrel," he said.
He said basic refining costs were now breakeven, compared to losses of around $1.50 per barrel last week.
Singapore's four refineries, which produce 1.3 million barrels per day (bpd), have been under pressure to cut their output amid the losses during the past month.
A source close to the 230,000-bpd Esso Singapore refinery told Reuters May 27 that the 230,000-bpd refinery had cut runs by 10-percent.
A company spokeswoman for Esso however declined to make any comment. The other refiners have not cut production, their spokesmen said.
The last round of refinery cuts was in January, when the refiners cut output between 8-20 percent.
But the latest relief to Singapore refiners is expected to be only short-lived, traders said.
By midday on Monday, Singapore product swaps were only marginally lower than Friday's levels.
Gas oil saw the largest losses -- but only of 35-40 cents a barrel -- to $24.05/$24.30 for June and July liftings.
But product traders said they expected prices to fall in line with crude and even more once the market warms up from the weekend.
"Prices could fall later even if crude recovers," said one trader.
High inventories of gas oil have already been weighing down prices as some refiners and producers have been forced to sell cargoes aggressively on the Singapore spot market.
Japanese middle distillate stocks are also high, adding further pressure to Asia's prices.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65-870-3086)
